etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Of お (honorific prefix) +‎ 嬢 (jō, “unmarried woman; daughter”) +‎ さん (honorific suffix)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Internationalism; see English organ. Probably from Portuguese órgão or English organ.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Internationalism of uncertain specifics, variously proposed to derive from English salad, French salade or Portuguese salada.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English papa or German Papa.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of レジスター (rejisutā), from English register.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 上(うわ) (uwa-, 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 上(うえ) (ue, “up; top”)) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “clothes; -wear”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 着(き)る (kiru, “to wear”)). The ki changes to gi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/putuka/ → /fut͡suka/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Analyzable as a compound of 二 (futsu, “two”, irregular reading, apparently a shift from expected reading futa) +‎ 日 (ka, “day”, uncommon variant only occurring in certain compounds of ancient derivation).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 二 (futa, “two”, used in counting) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”). Generally only found in instances of counting, as in ひとひふたひ (hitohi futahi, “one day, two days...”).
First cited in 1746.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From し (shi, “doing”, continuative form of する (suru, “to do”)) +‎ 事 (koto, “thing; stuff”). The koto reading for 事 changes to goto as an instance of rendaku (連濁). 仕 is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese ただし, from ただ (tada, “just, but”) +‎ し (shi, emphatic particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 商人 (MC syang nyin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shift from あきびと (akibito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Shift from あきびと (akibito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
Superficially あき (aki, “trade”) +‎ ひと (hito, “person”). Possibly Old Japanese.
Aki can also be found as the root of あきなう (akinau, “to trade”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 大 (tai, “big”) +‎ した (shita, “did, done”), the perfective of する (suru, “to do”), used here to indicate a state as opposed to an action.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
大(おお) (ō-, “large”) + 通(とお)り (tōri, “street”).
The tōri changes to dōri as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:

Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Emperor of Japan
Wikipedia
From Middle Chinese 天皇 (MC then hwang) with the original sense of “heavenly sovereign”.
The 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese. The ō reading for 皇 changes to nō as an instance of renjō (連(れん)声(じょう)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:天皇 (三皇)
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Heavenly Sovereign
Wikipedia
/ten kʷau/ → /tenkʷɔː/ → /tenkɔː/ → /tenkoː/
From Middle Chinese 天皇 (MC then hwang).
The 漢(かん)音(おん) (kan'on, literally “Han sound”) pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/sumeraɡi/ → /suberaɡi/
Shift from sumeragi below, with the nasal /m/ becoming a plosive /b/.
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
⟨sume1ro2ki1⟩ → */sumʲerəkʲi/ → */sumeraki/ → /sumeraɡi/
Possibly a shift from Old Japanese 天皇 (sume1ro2ki1).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
From 皇(すめら) (sumera-, prefix of praise and respect) + 君(きみ) (kimi, “lord, master → sovereign”). The kimi changes to gimi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
From 皇(すめら) (sumera-, prefix of praise and respect) + 尊(みこと) (mikoto, “Highness”).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:少女
Wikipedia ja
少女 (shōjo): a girl holding a puppy.
From Middle Chinese compound 少女 (MC syewX|syewH nrjoX|nrjoH). Compare modern Mandarin 少女 (shàonǚ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 乙 (oto, “young, little”) +‎ 女 (me, “female, girl”). Compare 男 (otoko, “man”), originally meaning "young boy".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of Old Japanese 常 (tsune, “constancy, permanence, forever”) +‎ に (ni, adverbial particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 座(ざ) (za, “seat”) + 布団(ふとん) (futon, “futon”). The futon reading for 布団 changes to buton as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
A compound of 座 (za, “sitting”) +‎ 敷 (shiki, “spreading, covering”), the stem noun form of verb 敷く (shiku, “to spread or lay out on the floor or ground”).
Japanese houses originally had wood floors, and mats or cushions called 座 (za) would be laid out (敷く (shiku)) for sitting upon. Tatami (畳) flooring did not become common until some time during the Muromachi Period, approximately 1337 to 1573.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined or borrowed from Chinese 營養 (yíngyǎng, “to nourish the body”) in the end of the Edo period. Both spellings 栄養 and 営養 were used until the establishment of 栄養研究所 (“the Institute of Nutrition”) in the Home Ministry in 1920 and the publication of 『栄養』 by Japanese scientist Tadasu Saiki in 1926, and thence 栄養 has been mainly used.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From earlier けはひ (kefafi), a compound of 気(け) (ke, “atmosphere, spirit; feeling, mood”) + 這(は)ひ (fafi, “creeping, crawling; spreading”, modern 這(は)い (hai); the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 這(は)ふ (fafu, “to crawl, to creep; to spread along the ground, to spread around”, modern 這(は)う (hau))).
The kanji 配 (“distribution”) was applied to the hai portion of the reading as an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Senses other than “thoughtfulness, consideration” are likely a shift from 気(け)配(はい) (kehai) above, using the kan'on reading of ki for 気.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: (This term, 気配, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
物(もの) (mono, “thing”) + 語(かた)る (kataru, “to tell, narrate”).
The kataru changes to gataru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 生け (ike, “making something come alive”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 生ける (ikeru, “to make something live”)) +‎ 花 (hana, “flower”). The hana changes to bana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 男 (otoko, “man; male”) +‎ の (no, appositional particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “child”).
First cited to a text from 1711.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally derived from 窄(すば)る (subaru, “to shrink, to get smaller”, archaic) + しい (-shii, adjectivizing suffix evoking the quality of the suffixed term), from the sense of “that which makes one shrink away”. Compare verbs 窄まる (subomaru), 窄める (subomeru). The kanji spelling is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).
The initial sense was strongly negative, and this usage continued until at least the mid-1800s in the Edo period, when the meaning shifted to a strong positive instead. Compare the development of English terrific, of strongly positive meanings, from terrify, of strongly negative meanings.
The modern kanji spelling could be considered an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/kamukapu/ → /kamuɡapu/ → /kanɡafu/ → /kanɡaferu/ (regular change for lower bigrade verbs) → */kangaweru/ (semi-regular sound shift for the /f/ phoneme; see ハ行(ぎょう)転(てん)呼(こ) (ha-gyō tenko)) → /kanɡajeru/ (semi-regular sound shift, collapsing /we/ into /je/) → /kanɡaeru/
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Ultimate derivation uncertain. Theories include:
Given the ancient kamugapu spelling, may be ka + mukau, where the ka is an unidentified prefixing element, or possibly 処(か) (ka), cognate with the こ (ko) in location determiners like ここ (koko, “here”) and どこ (doko, “where”), and the mukau is 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face something, to face a direction”, pronounced as mukapu in ancient times), from the sense of facing a thing or issue to thoroughly inspect it and think it over. The shift from mukapu to mugapu may be an example of assimilation and lenition, where the preceding /m/ softens the following /k/.
Alternatively, may be derived from the on'yomi of kan for the character 勘(かん) (kan, “intuition, perception”, prior to the development of the kana ん, this was spelled as kamu), plus some unknown element that was probably originally kapu, changing to gapu due to rendaku. The semantically relevant verbs with ancient readings of kapu, such as 変(か)える (kaeru, “to change”) all have to do with ideas of changing or turning, suggesting a possible original meaning of to change one's perception.
In addition, there are also obsolete readings of かうがふ (kaugafu, /m/ elided; compare the change of suffix む (-mu) to う (-u) or the usage of 柑(かん) (kan) in 柑(こう)子(じ) (kōji)), and かがふ (kagafu, /mu/ elided completely, as in man'yōgana or nanori usage of kanji like 安), giving further support for this etymology.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from older 田返す (tagaesu/takaesu), from 田 (ta, “cultivated field”) +‎ 返す (kaesu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 裏 (ura, “back, behind”) +‎ 切る (kiru, “cut”). The kiru changes to giru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From classical 見(み)ゆ (miyu), from 見(み)る (miru, “to see”) + ゆ (-yu, potential/passive suffix).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 目 (ma, “eye”) +‎ 見ゆ (miyu, “to be seen”, modern 見える).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The Classical Japanese conditional form of the verb 言う (iu, “to say, to speak”): 言わ (iwa, 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb 言う (iu)) +‎ ば (-ba, an inflectional suffix indicating the hypothetical condition).
